utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Barney Thomas, Rafael La Cruz and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone. Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Chad Mair, Daniela Tasic, Gregor Guy-Smith and Novak Lukic on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Could we move into private session just for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Prosecution calls Dr. Charles Kirudja, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you okay, Mr. Kirudja? Are you well this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as well as I can be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, can you begin please by providing us with your full name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: My name is Charles Kirudja. I was born in Kenya on April 20th, 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your current occupation is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I'm a retiree from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you give us, please, very briefly an indication of your background prior to your involvement in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Prior to my posting to Belgrade in April of 1992, I had been serving in various capacities at the United Nations beginning 1977. Those capacities included about seven years where I was involved in a field involving what national corporations and their influenced activities around the world. It was a special department of the UN at that time tasked with tracing all the affects, political, economic, and social at that time. Then I was transferred from that role to the department of finance and budget where I remained until about 1984, something like that. Then I was re-assigned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you were seven years in the other department starting from 1977.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, seven years, 1977 brings up to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I just said, just about 1984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought 1984 you were starting the new --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, 1984 is what I was going to tell you. And at that time, I was then assigned in the office of the controller and posted four years later to a department that had been created in 1988, following the withdrawal of the former Soviet Union from Afghanistan; and the United Nations had been tasked to pick up the pieces of the humanitarian crisis that had been created in Afghanistan. And responsible for that effort was the Late-Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan, who I was tasked to assist in organising that effort based in Geneva. And in that capacity, I was both the administrator of a fund where the international community had put their contributions, humanitarian and cash, for the effort. From Geneva I would be travelling around in Afghanistan, in the Soviet Union, in Iran, and in Pakistan because the effort around those countries were inclusive of the tasks that we were assigned to do. About 1989 or thereabouts, I was then returned back to the United Nations and given the task of dealing in the office of finance that dealt with peacekeeping activities, rather than the general financial and budgetary affairs of the UN. 1992, then I was posted to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before I talk about your postings in the former Yugoslavia, can you tell us what your academic qualifications are, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I graduated from the University of Nairobi in 1972, bachelor of commerce, specialising in management of business activities, operations research and management science. I then was given a scholarship by the Canadian foreign office and arrived in Canada 1972 at the University of York where I did a masters in business administration. Thereafter, I went to the University of Western Ontario where I graduated the PhD in business management operations research in 1977. And then the United Nations recruited me directly from London, Ontario, Canada, at the University of Western Ontario.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Moving now to your time in the Balkans, what was your first posting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We arrived in Belgrade where the mission headquarters was, and from there, I was posted on a fact-finding tour by bus from Belgrade to Osijek where Sector East. Across Osijek to Erdut where Sector East was based; and from Erdut, I was asked to proceed to Daruvar where Sector West was based, and from Daruvar I received a fax notifying me that I was to take over in Topusko in Sector North where I would be at that time acting as chief civil affairs officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before we go any further, Doctor, you have mentioned some areas which we should identify for the Trial Chamber, please. And I wonder, Your Honours, if I could have a map from the court binder up on the screen; it is 65 ter number 09234. At number 1 in the booklets, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: First of all, Doctor, do you recognise that map as one of the territories of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please tender the blank map as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The first area I'd like you to -- perhaps before I can you to mark these areas on the map, Doctor, you mentioned Sector North, Sector East, Sector West, can you explain what these sectors are? Not geographically what they are, but what they were actually -- why they were termed that way, what they were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The mission that the Security Council had authorised to these areas of the former Yugoslavia was based on an agreement that became known as the Vance Plan concluded between Belgrade and Zagreb and Dojt [phoen] as the basis of this mission by the Security Council. That Vance Plan had delineated areas of conflict within the former Republic of Yugoslavia, now known as Croatia, where the conflict of the parties at that time had an impact. Those areas designated by the Vance plan formed a number of designated "opstinas" or municipalities, if you like; and those areas spread all over parts of Croatia. And for administrative purposes when the UN began to implement the terms of the Vance Plan, they were designated as Sector East, which was in east Slavonia; Sector West, which was in west Slavonia; Sector North, which comprised a some of opstinas; and Sector South, which also comprised the remaining number of opstinas, which were all in what they used to call the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to ask Mr. Usher, please, to provide you with an electronic pen, and ask you, please, as best you can with the passage of time to mark roughly for us on the map before you on the screen those various sectors.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, this map with my old eyes has become very, very concentrated and it's very -- the density of it would make it hard for me, actually, to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: If you have a larger map where I can see the outlines of the opstinas that I have named, I could do that. Right now, I see a patch of green, white and all of the little lines in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Would it assist you, sir, if we enlarged the area of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. Could you do it again? I still can't read the names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we go to 65 ter number 09246, Your Honours, and that is map 7 in the booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And, Doctor, if that's still --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, I can begin to see the outlines of Sector North as -- Your Honour, if you are looking at this screen that I'm looking at, and if you can see my pen, there is the extension of the opstina called Kostanica that is to the west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see your pen unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You don't see my pen and I don't see what you are looking at, the same map. That map -- excuse me. I apologise, Your Honour. The opstina of Kostanica was part of the Sector North, and it comes down going westwards from Kostanica you pick up the opstina of Petrinja which was also part of Sector North, and then you come down to the opstina of a Dvor na Uni, which was in Sector North. West of Petrinja, you go to Glina, which was the opstina also inclusive of Sector North. And then from Glina you go westward, and you will see the opstina of Vrgin Most. I will name them when you can see them on the map, Vrgin Most and then as you proceed west of Vrgin Most, then you go to -- going down along the border south-west, you get to Slunj which was also a part of Sector North and part of the opstinas that are inclusive of Sector North. Vojnic and then going southwards, the border of Sector North, would have ended somewhere in Korenica and that was basically and roughly what was our Sector North. Northwards, there are some rivers that you can trace around, Mreznica, Kupa river, and westwards there should be another river. Maybe it is Korana, I've forgotten -- maybe it's Korana. I've forgotten the name. Those were roughly the boundaries of Sector North, and it was that area where we were located. My office being at Topusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Your Honours, could we tender the blank map, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The blank map number 7 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, what was the position that you held when you first -- when you were first posted to Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: At that time, the position had been described the chief civil affairs officer; and shortly thereafter, it was revised to civil affairs coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: From 1992 to 1994, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: During that period, were you or was your area of responsibility Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And you were posted physically in Sector North throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: My duties were to ensure that the terms of the Vance Plan as endorsed by the Security Council as the core functions of the mission were implemented and implemented in full. Therefore, I had the responsibility alongside the military sector commander to advise the initial aspect of that mandate which were all military. And it was military in the sense that the terms of the Vance Plan required that there be a total demobilisation, decommissioning of military materiel and personnel. And also to ensure that all military personnel are put out of business, so to speak, except for the police which had been made in the terms of the Vance Plan an exception to that. The only authority that were to remain in all the sector activities was the authority of civilians who ran the opstina beginning with the mayors, as well as the police. The police were to be reintegrated and made reflective of the communities that occupied the place before, and they were only to carry light weapons with their, quote, side-arms at that time. Then the mandate, if all went well, all weapons had to be locked into common storage was known as a double-key system, where the UN would take control of those weapons along with the local authorities. The mandate envisaged from there we would be tasked with ensuring a safe and voluntary return of the people who had been displaced from those areas. And for that, our part of the mission had police contingent, UN police contingent, that we would work with to ascertain that the conditions for voluntary return were taken hold on the ground. And finally, we had to render humanitarian assistance for all those who had been affected during that war and after. Basically that was the responsibility that the civil affairs coordinator had, and the rest was the responsibility of the military commander for the implementation of the military aspects of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did your duties, therefore, require you to deal directly with the military leaderships of the forces concerned?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, the earlier part of the mission was almost exclusively a military endeavour because when we arrived in the area, the combatant, the people who were fighting were still in their foxholes. There were tanks facing each other. There were people armed eye to eye across the confrontation lines. Most of the houses and residences had been destroyed, and people had already run away from the area. So the only thing that was -- the only activity that was there was a military activity. Our duty was, therefore, to immediately engage all the warring parties on both sides of the confrontation line from Sisak through Karlovac to Ogulin to Rijeka; and we had to go immediately identify all the military command on the Serb side and on the Croat side; and as time went on in March or so on the Bosnian border that was bordering Sector North. So most of our time from April all through to June or July was heavily a military involvement of the sector commander and myself to try to achieve the earlier goal, I said, of getting the parties to demobilise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You spoke earlier of the two signatories of the Vance Plan having been Zagreb and Belgrade. Who were the military forces, what were the military forces engaged in the conflict that you were concerned with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I'm sure you were aware this was originally one country called Yugoslavia, and when these conflicts took the turn they did necessitating the Vance Plan, there was a military known as JNA. JNA was a national military. The JNA deployed in the areas that became the United Nations protected area, Sector North and Sector South formed one military command, and that military command was based in Bihac. And that military command, I believe, was the 10th Corps. And the 10th Corps was based in the -- and the command was in Bihac. And at that time, Lieutenant-General Spiro Nikovic was in command. So most of our earliest engagement began with him, to identify all the command structure and the deployment of the military in Sector North. Specifically, we learned he had divided or the 10th Corps had divided Sector North into two regional command. One command was known as Banja, and the command was located at that time when we arrived in Petrinja. And there was the command called Kordun that was based at the time we arrived somewhere near Topusko, somewhere in the wooded area, near Topusko that was the command and a bit of it in Vojnic but mostly it was called Kordun. Part of Sector North also involved Lika command, which took the whole opstina of Slunj and part of Korenica and Plaski. Plaski was another opstina that I didn't mention in my earlier. So we had to identify who was in command, and then because the Security Council also had made the mandate of UNPROFOR at that time to be within the area that I'm referring in Sector North across the line of confrontation, there were the Croatian side of the military. So we had to identify on the Croatian side who was in command. And we did, ran the command from Sisak through Karlovac and then across to the side that are called on Ogulin side running all the way to Rijeka there was a military command based in Rijeka at that time. So we did identify all of those command. On the Croatian side, they had formed, there were much more organised since there were the signatories with Belgrade and they had been recognised as an independent country so they were overtly, more clearly organised when we arrived and committed to dealing with UNPROFOR and they had a commander in Sisak, General Budnji [phoen]. And in Karlovac, they had a commander, but at that time they had put the entire organisation under one civilian leader whom we dealt with where he would come into a room with his military command, and that civilian was the Deputy Prime-Minister Ramljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just going back to the JNA command for a moment, did you come across a Colonel Cedomir Bulat?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, Cedo Bulat was the commander of the Kordun wing of the 10th Corps in Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was he there throughout your period in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, he was the longest serving of all the commanders from when I arrived to when the sector was taken over by the Croats by force. He remained in that capacity the longest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Once you had identified the appropriate people to deal with within the respective commands, within the respective command structures of the two armies, did you then engage each side in accordance with what you were required to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We did our best, under very trying circumstances. I can't say we achieved most of what we started out, but I believe we did achieve a lot of what we had started out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: How long were the JNA engaged in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: General Spiro Nikovic was tasked with the responsibility of demobilising his entire command. He engaged us from the time we arrived, I arrived in April there, to a certain date in May, I believe, which I don't recall the date, when we had reached an agreement, both on the Croatian side and on the Serb side that the warring parties would withdraw their forces to a designated distance from the confrontation line. And the Serbs insides the UNPA had been given a general order that said something like anyone of the commanders that was not indigenous in that area, meaning born there but serving with the JNA, were to be recalled from their command, and leave only what they began to call Territorial Defence forces commanded in more or less the same structure, but under the control of those who were indigenous, meaning born in the area. That included Cedo Bulat, who was born somewhere near Vrgin Most, originated from there. I don't know for sure that he was born there, but I know his house and family, where it was. But on the Banja command, the general who was there, at the time, had to leave because he had originated from Montenegro. And in his place, eventually, we had a series of commanders taking over very quickly but the last and longest serving there was Colonel Tabak [phoen] in Banja. That particular situation for Spiro ended when he himself, Spiro Nikovic was also a Montenegrin, but he didn't complete or see to completion the negotiation of the demobilisation that he had reached with us. He called us one evening and we met in his office in Bihac, and we abruptly announced that he had been recalled, and he had to hand-over to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Besides your dealings with military authorities to carry out your own mandate, were you required as part of your duties to meet with any of the political authorities in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. We had also for the purposes of achieving that requirement of the Vance Plan that the area returned to the control of civilian authorities, meaning the mayors and police. So I had to go to every capital of each opstina and identify who was in civil control, as well as in police and military control.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In your dealings either with the military or the political authorities, did you encounter any articulated concept of a greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Remember, you come into a situation where people are still engaged in communal hostility, and the first question is they want to engage you is the righteousness of their course: Why they are fighting. When we ask, Why are you fighting, why are you fighting each other; invariably you will hear, we no longer can live together and we have to go our separate ways. And if you ask who are we in a country that was previously a homogenous country, you quickly understood whether the speaker was, we the Serbs and on the other side the Croats. And if you come down southwards towards the border with Bosnia, there were the Muslims. So we, depending on the speaker, was we the Croats, we the Serbs, and the Muslims don't enter into that kind until much later, you don't hear about we can't live together from the Muslim side. Mostly you heard that from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And would you hear that from the military authorities or the political authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Most of the military officers you meet are not given to giving speeches or explain why they are doing things. You heard it mostly from the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were the political authorities with whom you dealt all based in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, as I mentioned to you, a good part of the controls of the military was in Bihac, meaning the part of the opstinas, in Bosnia running all the way from Bosanski Novi to Krupa, to Velika Kladusa to Bihac; and these were people we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The Serb articulation or the articulation by the political authorities with whom you dealt of this concept of a greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object because that mis-characterizes the gentleman's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can rephrase that question because it does paraphrase what the doctor is saying, and I appreciate that that can cause some difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. And I think so far the doctor said we, the Croats; we, the Serbs and much later; we, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, you spoke of -- and I'm just talking about the Serbs at the moment, about how they would speak of the inability to live in cohabitation, if you like, with the other ethnic groups in Sector North. Was this a theme that carried on throughout your time in Sector North, at least as far as the Serbs were concerned?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, and let me clarify. When I say from the military side you don't hear that particularly said. That didn't mean it didn't come out in a different way. It did come in a different way. The military, for example, if I ask them why are you fighting, in one of my written testimony, I do give an account of Spiro Nikovic explaining to us what he was fighting for and why he stopped where he stopped. I mentioned Sector North stops in the northern opstinas of Vrgin Most and Petrinja going across, they were the confrontation lines stopped around rivers, Mreznica, Kupa, and Korana on the west side going down to Slunj. He said, I could take - I remember - I could have taken Zagreb, I could have taken Karlovac; but we didn't have to do that because those cities were predominantly Croats, why do we need to take them? So we needed a natural area that was mostly Serb and that mostly Serb was in those opstinas. When he was explaining on the Bosnian side why are you fighting there also, he would say, for example, most of those areas, 80 percent are Serb, so we need to control areas which are mostly Serb. Doesn't go beyond that. But you could see that it not too different a concept when the civilians vouch we can't any longer live together.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Engaged in this role in Sector North, were you ever required to engage the FRY authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not from Sector North. I later on got to engage the FRY authorities when I was posted in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. You spoke of the soldiers who were left behind from the JNA, if I can use that term, but the ones who remained as those born on the territory forming a Territorial Defence force, and defence of what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: As he knew well, that Vance Plan made no distinction when they said we want all the weapons decommissioned and put in control -- in storage points controlled between the UN forces and the local authorities. They were not to be removed from the area, but were to be put in storage. However, he explained, General Spiro Nikovic when we were negotiating that there are still dangers that our people faced if we pulled out. The Territorial Defence forces would be left with sufficient -- sufficient weapons so they can defend themselves. And those weapons included heavy weapons like artillery, armoured vehicle, tanks, all except air force kind of weapons that would project fighting beyond those areas. Those weapons would be pulled and taken by the JNA as it was as they were pulling out. I remember General Spiro was very honest in his attempt to deal with us and he would provide at our request an explanation of why he was doing what he was doing. At one point, he did tell us, bear in mind, for our own understanding we didn't know what was unfolding every week after week and about May he says, There is a new reality in the former Yugoslavia, and that new reality, he said, was that you -- the former Yugoslavia is going to break up into six republics and he proceeded to name them. Those republics he named were: Serbia and Montenegro in one rump, remainder of the former Yugoslavia: Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, and Republika Srpska and Republic Serbian Krajina, RSK. So what he called the remaining is what is today the new republics except those two RS and RSK, which he expected to be separate republics. And that made it understandable why he would insist certain weapons be left for the defence of our people, left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When the JNA did withdraw, did they leave the weapons behind as he said they would?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, they were left behind, and we did collect them and put them in storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When did you move -- or when did you leave Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Late 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And that was -- and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I was named Chief of Staff for the civilian side of the mission in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Short. Because from there I was asked to proceed as the delegate of the special representative of the sector general to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And did you take up that post?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And would that have been -- do you know exactly when you began that -- commenced that post?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Really I've forgotten a lot of things especially about when I did these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If I suggested August 1994, does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what were your -- first of all, Mr. Akashi was the special representative to the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He was the second. The first one was Stoltenberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: But you as delegate were reporting to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Was reporting to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: To Akashi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what were your duties or what did you expect your duties to be as delegate of the special representative in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A lot has -- had changed by that August 1994 in the UNPAs, but the signatories and the drivers of the reality going on their remained still the authorities in Belgrade and the authorities in Zagreb. The course of events in the sectors still was being discussed, driven, negotiated, if you like. There was a contact group of countries that were assisting the parties and the UN. There was a bigger forum based in Geneva known as the ICFY, International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, still also conducting the events going on in the sectors as well as in the broader area known as Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Secretary-General and the UN was involved in all of that, and the special representative of the Secretary-General needed to engage the authorities in Belgrade as well as in Zagreb. When he would engage the authorities in Belgrade, it was my responsibility to arrange and be his arm in engaging the authorities on that score. There was also a no-fly resolution against Yugoslavia, Security Council Resolution 761, that also required us to monitor and engage the former -- the authorities in Belgrade. Lastly, there was the question of the Prevlaka peninsula which fell within the country then known as -- republic then known as Montenegro but part of what was left as Yugoslavia. My responsibility, therefore, was to engage both the leadership in Belgrade, at that time President Milosevic, and the leadership in Montenegro, at that time President Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, you've mentioned a couple of groups or organisations that I should probably get you to explain just a little bit more for us. The first is the contact group and the contact group plan. Can you just describe what those were, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A lot went on in the sectors but the sum effect of what was going on by the time we are talking about in August 1994 was an idea that Belgrade and Zagreb were pursuing, and that was to move in measured steps in resolving the conflict in the former part of Croatia that there was fighting, and grant those sectors, the authorities in those sectors sort of semi-autonomy, autonomy within Croatia. And to negotiate those -- that outcome of some autonomy for those -- for the Serbs who lived in those areas. The contact group formed around some of the most influential countries like Germany. I mentioned Germany because the leader of the contact group at that time was the ambassador from Germany. There was United States and there was Russia, and I forget what the other countries were but there were six of them. And that was what the contact group was trying to reach and the negotiated outcome and autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what was the -- geographically what was the compass of the contact group plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Basically was to have -- since it never happened, it was a much negotiated, argued, or debated concept. If there were to be an autonomy, what would be the nature of that. Since it never happened, it is hard to give you a concrete thing because whatever was being proposed was at one point being opposed by the other side. So whatever it was that didn't happen is simply there was no autonomy, and when the autonomy and the discussions around autonomy failed, then Croatia took action that resulted to what you know as an overrun of all the sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If the JNA had retreated from Croatia leaving behind the Serb Territorial Defence force in respect of those disputed areas, why was it necessary to engage the FRY authorities in relation to the contact group plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The Serbs who took over control of sectors north, south, west, and east ended up basically not following the Vance Plan and begun activities aimed at making reality of their goal of an RSK Republika Serbian Krajina in what was a territory that Croatia had always eventually projected that they had control over that area. In order for us to deal with the events in that area, with Croatia insisting that this is its territory and it had to proceed in a manner that we can agree with whether it's semi-autonomy or full return to autonomy, that's -- we have to be engaged. So the engagement of Zagreb is clear from that point. But for the engagement of the Serbs who began to control and project that control inside those areas, the question was are they doing it all by themselves without anybody's assistance because this begun as an integrated Yugoslavia; and, therefore, there were under the control of Belgrade in so many ways from the fact that starting with the soldiers. These soldiers whether they were first JNA or they had transformed themselves to TDF, they were drawing some pay, some support of all kind including money from, the question was did that flow, did the payment from did it stop from Belgrade. Our position was it didn't stop. The communications lines when they wanted to communicate, where did these communications lines originate from? The currency, the money, where did this originate from? Therefore there was an umbilical linkage always to Belgrade. Therefore, the outcome of all what would happen in those areas, Belgrade was always a major player and they had to be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When you did engage Belgrade on these issues, were they prepared to engage? Did they accept that they needed to engage?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Very clearly they always had like Zagreb, their own policy view about what they wanted to see happen there. That eventually begun to digress from what their kin and kith who were in those territories were doing. Towards the end, I go towards the end of the process, Belgrade with Milosevic in charge at that time had already reached a policy agreement that whatever would happen in those areas had to be settled through peaceful negotiation and no military. They did not never changed that they wanted to see a negotiated outcome, no military. Events of course were not always totally controllable by either side. When there was a reality of an RSK, there was other events happening in and around Pale about the Republika Srpska and the two realities had a lot of common confluence around and if not a common policy. In the end, there did emerge a deviation because the negotiated process never bore fruit. Even if the Belgrade people wanted it to bear fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, just before I leave this point and I've strayed from where we were at a little while ago, but the second organisation you mentioned which might require some explanation is ICFY, the International Conference on Former Yugoslavia. Can you explain, first of all, if I've got the name right; and secondary, who were the members of this group and what was their function?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Very briefly, this was an umbrella forum on one side co-chaired or co-driven by the UN on one side and by the European Union on the other. And the co-chairs initially of that organisation were Lord Owen representing the European Union side and Stoltenberg representing the United Nations side. There was also recognition that there were issues that involved the entire former Yugoslavia that were not localised simply in sectors or in Bosnia or just Croatia and the Serbia alone, there were issues that were much broader. And the forum was to kind of put a lasting umbrella to the outcome of the solutions that were being sought in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as in Croatia. To that extent they were engaged on the ground with us. I did meet on the ground with Lord Owen. He had come there several times to be informed about what was going on on the ground. Cyrus Vance himself did come, but he was basically representing the contact group as the original inspirer of this Vance Plan but in the context of the contact group. But and also in broader involvement of his own country in the process, and that would, of course, put him at every aspect of that including ICFY. Therefore, the group that was in ICFY would endorse negotiations that came from the ground as valid. Specifically, the result of the contact group which we spoke. At one time, we were given to understand, we were close to getting an agreement for autonomy that Serbs led by Martic at that time and the Croatian government would agree. Most of those negotiations were not even in the former Yugoslavia. We would take delegate, people representing both the Serbs and the Croat into Geneva where we had many, many meetings with these groups, under the ICFY because the headquarters -- that's where ICFY was and at times also in Vienna. That was the overall process of validation of attempted solutions to the issues that were on the ground arising from the various flash points in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In general terms during your posting in Belgrade, which of the FRY authorities did you most often deal with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Most of the times I did deal with the FRY authorities over issues that involved the sectors and that was President Milosevic. At that time he was the president of Serbia, but he still was the main player. As you know, there was another president for the former Yugoslavia jointly meaning Republic of Serbia and Montenegro. He was still the president of Serbia when we were dealing with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause there for a moment, Doctor. Could you just explain that dynamic a little bit for the Trial Chamber. We have the president of the FRY, on the one hand; and the president of Serbia on the other hand. Can you just explain why it was that Milosevic was the key player?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This was never understood in the media, but it was always understood in the international community where anybody who was involved from the leadership of other countries that would come in Belgrade and they would meet not Lilic; I never met him so, therefore, I don't even remember very much because it was the president of Serbia whom we met with. There was a prime minister in both -- also of Yugoslavia, that I remember because his Deputy Simic we did meet with. However, the control of the reality de facto, I'm not talking about de jure; de facto authority, de facto influence was with the president of Serbia at that time, Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was that the situation as well prior to your arrival in Belgrade in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, even before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was it the position when you left Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When was that, can you recall when you departed Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Presumably -- let me ask you another question. On how many occasions would you say you've met Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I actually never kept count, but I did meet him so many times, and each meeting was not a short meeting, it was always long meetings lasting anywhere between four and six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You've spoken of this theme of greater Serbia emerging during your time in Sector North --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again that mis-characterizes the gentleman's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to find the appropriate passage in the transcript, so I can get that right. I wonder if it would be an appropriate time to take the break now, and I can pick up on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's an appropriate time we'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned that during your time in Belgrade, it became apparent that Milosevic's preference was for a negotiated settlement rather than an military option in response to the contract group plan, for example. At what point did that preference on the part of Milosevic become apparent?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it you mean his own personal knowledge of that, or are we talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He is just asking the question. And the witness will tell whether he has any personal knowledge of it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that, but the way the question is framed, it would seem that the point is a point in time that would either become a truth or a non-truth based upon -- and by that I'm talking about time, based upon what this witness say, so there may well be other information that his preference, meaning Milosevic's preference, existed in a much earlier time or not at a much earlier time. I think Mr. Thomas understand the thrust of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It says when it -- at what time did it become apparent, so it may have existed long before it became apparent, all the lawyer wants to know is when it became apparent to the witness, if at all. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, when did it first become apparent to you that Mr. Milosevic's preference was for a negotiated settlement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic himself said so. If you ask me whether he had said it before I heard it, I wouldn't know that. But he did say in several instances where there was an issue, there was an issue, for example, when the first action taken Croatian authorities to retake western Slavonia. We had a meeting called by Mr. Akashi because of that event. There was an incident where we met with him when, for example, the NATO shot down some planes flown by some RSK officials from the field in Udbina. During this event, there was violence created over an issue like shooting down the plane or taken by force, by the Croatian authorities, western Slovenia. In instances, I'm not saying it's only limited to those instance, Milosevic would always in addressing the UN delegations repeat, This is a preference I have that there be a negotiated solution. And he believed and he repeated many times passionately, that if he wasn't, I remember words to the effect: If you left us in the same room, myself and president Tudjman, we could agree to negotiate this solution. But I understand you would say there are forces at all sides that are opposed to this negotiated solution, and he termed those forces as forces that want a war solution, specifically in both RSK and Bosnia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are forces which are intent on having -- having a war solution. But he would also hasten to say, They will not succeed. In the case, he will say, look, for example, the supporters of such a war option like the member of parliament aligned with [indiscernible]. He lost his position recently in advancing this war position. He repeated this, so it's not a secret that he said that. The time sequence of when he said any of these things I have referred to, Your Honour, these events took place a long, long time, and I can't give you an exact time sequence about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, you referred to one of your topics of engagements with the FRY authorities as being the no-fly zone, and I think you mentioned Security Council Resolution 781. Can you just explain what the no-fly zone is or was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was a much older resolution coming about the same time the resolution enabling the mission started. The same time when the Security Council was authorising this nation to get ahold of the events that were unfolding in the whole of Yugoslavia at that particular time. They wanted also to ensure that the seat of Yugoslavian power, which was then Belgrade, didn't project its advantage in fighting forces, especially their force, to project beyond where it was. So they were forbidden to fly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please have Exhibit 65 ter 02190 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, you can see from the title that we are looking at Security Council Resolution 781 adopted on the 9th of October, 1992 by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I see on the B/C/S side it's Resolution 780 of 6 of October, 1992. Instead of 9th of October, 1992 and instead of being -- okay. Now we've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The relevant passage that I'd like to draw everyone's attention to is on page 2 of both version, please. Numbered paragraphs 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, do you see paragraphs 1 and 2 establishing the ban on military flights and also enabling the United Nations protection force to monitor compliance with that ban?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are those the relevant parts of the resolution -- are these what is relevant to your description of the no-fly zone? Are we talking about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, the ban is on all military flights in the air-space of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is apparent enough. But I am interested also in paragraph 2 which enables: "The protection force to monitor compliance including the placement of observers when necessary at air-fields in the territory of the former Yugoslavia." Was UNPROFOR able to place the necessary observers at those relevant installations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah, we had a contingent of United Nations military observers in the control rooms at a Surcin airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And where is Surcin airport?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What was the function of those UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Actually, I never went inside there, myself; but they would brief me routinely. They were to observe what was going on there for whatever was in violation of the resolution as they interpreted it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you know specifically what they were looking at or looking for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Unless there was an event like an event that I describe in one of my reports, routinely I wouldn't know what they were looking for. But if there was a specific event like the one that is discussed in one of my reports, I know what they were looking for. They were looking for the tapes of -- or radar to confirm whether or not that event took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Let me ask the question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Thomas. I do hate to interrupt. If you could do us a kindness here. Mr. Perisic is having difficulty reading on the screen the exact portion that you were discussing with Mr. Kirudja. If you don't mind terribly just reading it out so that he gets the precise language, I'd appreciate it. I do apologise for interrupting. I really am sorry, I was just given a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suggest you also talk via the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I apologise to the Bench for that, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's no problem, Your Honours, I can read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The relevant passage is, I'm reading the numbered paragraphs 1 and 2 in the English version, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suspect what Mr. Guy-Smith is saying is that the B/C/S is not numbered. Therefore, Mr. Perisic is finding it difficult to pin-point the exact paragraph that you were reading. So reading the English version is not likely to be helpful to him, maybe. If you can point at the B/C/S one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I think, sir, the relevant -- it would appear, sir, that it is the starting at the fifth paragraph on the page that's on the screen at the moment. But I will defer of course to my native B/C/S speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, the only problem is that the B/C/S version is not numbered like the English version. I believe the general will be able to follow now, but perhaps it would be a good idea -- it's exactly as was explained. It's the fifth paragraph in the B/C/S. I believe Mr. Thomas identified the paragraph correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, were the UNMOs stationed at Surcin airport?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And was their function to monitor this resolution as or monitor the ban as set out in this resolution?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And was their task to report to you or to others if there were any breaches of the ban?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Their task was to report what they observed through a well-defined channel among which was their own superior which the UNMO line went to the chief military observer, and then to the force commander. And then on the civilian side, they would brief from the local to the headquarter civilian line.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was there an appreciation on the part of the FRY authorities that access needed to be given to the UNMOs to undertake that task?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They did it rather willingly and effortlessly considering there was also a sanction resolution, not this one, against the remaining Yugoslavia. They, relatively speaking, they were very forthcoming about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just on that a topic, was compliance or otherwise with Resolution 781, this resolution, something that would be relevant when it came to deciding whether or not sanctions should be lifted or extended?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I don't recall the sequence of -- I think the sanctions of the resolution came after since this is in 1992. I think the sanctions, I'm not sure, you can check that, and I don't know whether this resolution influenced it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if I may just get clarification, Doctor. When you said there were sanctions against the remaining Yugoslavia, what do you mean by remaining Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the old well-known Yugoslavia fell apart and Slovenia went its way, Croatia went -- began to go its way, Bosnia-Herzegovina voted to secede, then the authorities reconstituted Yugoslavia and retained the name Yugoslavia to mean the joint what was known as Montenegro and what was known in Serbian, the old resolution formed the new Yugoslavia although they didn't use the label "new."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that what was called the FRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was not actually recognised by the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we tender as Exhibit please Security Council Resolution 781, which is the one on the screen says 65 ter 02190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just so I can clarify a comment you just made, Doctor, about the sanctions resolution, could we have P00202 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you will see that we are looking at Resolution 757 adopted on the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we look, Your Honours, please, at page 3 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you look under paragraph 4 there, Doctor, we see a number of sanctions referred to. They spill over on to the next page, and please tell if you need to go on to the next page, but is this what you refer today as the sanctions resolution?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Once the sanctions resolution was imposed, was the lifting of the sanctions or the reduction of the sanctions something that was upper most in the mind of the FRY authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: To your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And part of the reason why I remembered it because in the execution of the no-fly resolution, they would remind me as a representative of the UN, a point I always noted, Look, we are trying to do the best under the sanctions resolution. Like these machines require spare parts, and we can't do it so easily with our hands so tied by the sanctions resolution. Yes, it was foremost in their mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You've referred to the authorities saying that they needed spare parts for certain machines. What machines are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Particularly on this incident that I referred to, the UNMOs would go into the radar room and find out some equipment, I don't know exactly what equipment they reported, not functioning; and they are asking why is this not functioning, and state spare parts problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are we going back now to the UNMOs monitoring the no-fly zone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In early February 1995, did you become aware of possible violations of the no-fly zone by the FRY?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Perhaps before I move on to that topic, in addition to the no-fly resolution, were there other issues concerning the border between the FRY and the Republika Srpska at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, Republika Srpska was not something we as the UN knew as an existence. If you mean with Bosnia-Herzegovina was the border between -- a recognised border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that border is actually defined by the river Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: At the time of these possible violations, early February 1995, was the border between the FRY and Bosnia-Herzegovina open?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Who had closed it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The authorities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And when had they closed it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Why did they close it, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I learned why they exposed -- and the reason you see a reluctance in answering why, is because this mandate and the whole issue involving that border, the FRY authorities made sure that it doesn't involve the UN. It involved the European Union and the FRY authorities, and whatever may have been official reasons involving it didn't come my way. I can only, of course, tell you my understanding since I needed to understand what was going on what was it about. It was about Milosevic being taken to task many times when he met in the international community including ourselves that there were movements of materiel and personnel involved in the conflict in Yugoslavia across that border, and this wasn't helping. Taking him to task many times this way, he said, if you don't believe us, we will close the border to ensure this doesn't happen except for humanitarian -- humanitarian supplies which obviously we couldn't deny passage. And then from there on, the monitors he agreed would be supplied by the European Union, and he set up this organisation for monitoring, and it was headed by our former chief military observer in his capacity as a European, General Pellnas from Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you know until what date the border was closed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: From your own observations and your own dealings in Belgrade at the time, did you have any observations as to whether this was effective, ineffective, whether anything materially changed with the closing of the border?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The simple answer to that is that it was really not my responsibility even to find out whether it was effective or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The monitors that were supplied to monitor this border closure were supplied by whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to move now to these helicopter flights that were -- or this issue which arose in early February 1995. Before we go on to some documents dealing with that, can you just generally explain to the Trial Chamber what occurred?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Very generally, and I would -- if Your Honour agree, I would like to see that report. It's about three pages, to refresh my memory about it. It is a report I wrote to Mr. Akashi, and unlike other reports, it's a coded cable. Coded meaning it did carry lots of sensitivity in its content, so I wouldn't have sent it in an ordinary way. There are routine reports that we made. That was not a routine report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please have 65 ter 03283 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, 02?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, 03283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise that as the report that you wrote to Mr. Akashi on the subject?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before we go into some aspects of that report, what prompted this report? What was the first information you received, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This mission has -- it was a complex United Nations mission with reporting channels that involved the total sources from civilians, from police, from military observers. Military reports from people on the ground are daily sitreps wherein prior to this report, and they are circulated to all senior management, we get our supply of reports on a daily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, can you explain what sitreps are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Situation reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Daily situation reports. And those come from all channels. So prior to this report, a flash report comes that a contingent of UN forces. The Dutch contingent specifically in Srebrenica reported a contingent of helicopters that flew across the border towards their direction, towards their base. When military sitreps come that way, they just report the facts and not the reasons, not anything. And of course, it comes back later to what was this all about. UN Belgrade, what this all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: At the same time, what was happening to the UNMOs at Surcin airport who were tasked to police the no-fly zone or the ban on military flights into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Their sit report were report on this particular day we couldn't go in, we were not allowed to go in. We normally can go routinely to observe. Their sit report says we were not there, we could not go, we were not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To go in where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the airport, to the control room.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn, Your Honours, please, to page -- in the same document, to page 9 of the English version and page 11 of the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise that as an annex to your report dealing with the restriction of movement to the radar room that the UNMOs encountered?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Separated from the report, I can only assume because again it's a long time ago, it's an attachment I didn't write. So in and of itself couldn't be recognisable by me unless it is physically attached to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand, I understand. Could you read the document quietly to yourself and tell us if that accords with your recollection of what occurred at the time.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I've read part of the front page, and it is now clear reminiscent of what I was trying to say earlier, that the UNMOs at this time, it's Colonel Goodmanson [phoen]. Colonel Goodmanson comes to my office, and he is reporting this incident, and this is what happened. It was unusual in the sense in which there was unfriendliness on the part of the authorities over this issue which was unusual. I said earlier there always was a friendly and cooperative relationship until this occasion. And because it didn't -- it stood out from the ordinary way unnecessarily aggressive and argumentative on a simple issue can we go in where we have always gone in to observe what we have always observed. That is reflected in the report that you saw earlier in one of the paragraphs where I'm thinking this was also made purposely so that we can take note. My report itself characterises it as an incident staged so that we can take note.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand. This page deals with events or restriction of movement on the 2nd of February. I want to also turn, please, to page 8 -- sorry, Your Honours, the previous page before this one in the English. Thank you. And two pages back in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, this is also an annex to the same report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: First of all, there will be some terms that might need further clarification. If you look at the title, "Summary of ROM ..." The previous report, if it's of any assistance, dealt with restriction of movement. Would ROM appear to be an abbreviation of the same thing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And Surcin ATC?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Where does it occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Is ATC, do you know what ATC would stand for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The report appears to deal with matters involving staff at air-traffic control, could that be the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you look down at the entry on the 9th and 10th of February, 1995, "Oral protest forwarded to SLO air FRY".

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah, senior liaison officer. SLO, senior liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next entry begins with "DSMO."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Deputy -- senior military observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. On the seconds line, at the end, we have "but LO off" and then a name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, do you recognise that document as what it purport to be, namely a summary of restriction of movement over those days?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Again part of ordinary sitrep, that's what you would recall a situation report, they did that routinely every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we move back to page 1 of the document, of the exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 1 introduces the steps that you took in response to these possible violations, and the authorities with whom you spoke. Again, just a couple of abbreviations and acronyms that we might need your assistance on. Firstly, the third line after Colonel Vuksic, we have, "Responsible to JA General Kovacevic." JA standing for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And was that an abbreviation that you yourself used consistently in your reports and in your dealings?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. And the second to last line in that paragraph, "The SRFC in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Is the senior representatives of the force commander, a military official located in my office at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Part of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 2, you summarise the response of the FRY authorities to the allegation regarding these cross border helicopter flights. What I'm interested in is paragraph 3, which is on the next page of both documents, please, Your Honours. You make two requests in subparagraph (a) and subparagraph (b) to the FRY authorities. The first appears self-explanatory that access be restored to the UNMOs to the radar screens.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you just assist the Trial Chamber why you made the second request the tapes of radar observations, and any relevant flight logs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Paragraph (b) you also requested that the tapes of radar observations and any relevant flight logs from the period 1-4 February be provided to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Because this matter had reached the Security Council as the previous paragraph show. The previous paragraphs show this matter was now a Security Council matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You are talking about paragraph 3 on the same page?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I had on instruction gone to see Mr. Cicanovic about this matter and registered the point made at (a) on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not said here and there had been decision there would be a military investigation to ascertain these claims about the airport. And part of that investigation involved if there are planes doing a no-fly violation in a situation where there is a radar system, was it captured by the radar? If not, why not. Central to that investigation would be the tapes that were kept by the FRY authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. And I should also highlight that in paragraph 3, you also make the point that the present information made it inconclusive, at that time at least, as to whether or not helicopter flights had crossed the international border or could be identified as belonging to or associated with any of the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: At that point did you have any reason to dispute the reports from those in Srebrenica who had reported the flights?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I was never in the habit of disputing military observers or police observers on the ground saying on this day and this day we saw that. That for me wouldn't have been a disputable matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I tender, we needn't tender the whole document. The page that is we've referred to will be sufficient. Those are --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might. I suggest we do tender the whole document because there might be some further questions about this particular document, so rather than going through some of the difficulties we have with incomplete documents being tendered, I would suggest we tender the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many pages is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In total, sir, I think it's 10 or 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your response to your learned friend?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The -- sir, the Prosecution has no need of the other pages. They flesh out matters already referred to in summary and the report to which we have referred. I have no difficulty putting the entire document in, however, if that's ultimately going to be a lot easier than going through the process of being under cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document then is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we please have 65 ter 03282 on the screen, please. Sorry, Your Honours, I think I've got the wrong document. Sorry, 65 ter 03281. My apologies. No again the wrong one. Sorry, Your Honours. It will take me a second. 03280. My apologies again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It is. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, you will recognise this as a further code cable you sent to Mr. Akashi on the 16th of February on this issue?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You begin by stating in the first paragraph that UNMO access to the radar screens has been restored.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Can you increase it, sir, please. My aging eyes are struggling on this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And the tapes have been -- or the tapes are available for analysis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Why did you make the comment that you can't be too sure or that it would be your bet that the tapes will contain nothing implicating the FRY authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: In the first place, this precedes several meetings I had including one with the FRY authorities. And you showed that in an earlier thing. You also showed that they said it didn't happen. And if you want the tapes, you can have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I knew the fact that they are going to give me the tape, the tapes won't be incriminating. They are coming from the government sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I don't know any governments that hands over incriminating records. I'm speaking in general now. We were given the tapes willingly with the proviso that we didn't do this, and, therefore, I was sure that it would be a big surprise if they were proved wrong by the tapes. That is why my bet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If that were the case, why do you make the next comment, the first comment in paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which comment, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry Your Honours: "Confidential local sources here leave little doubt that those flights happened and were from the JA."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That was me trying to corroborate what our own soldiers were saying. So the local people say yeah, they were, they happened. But they were not captured on tape. Therefore, the rest of the thing is how come they weren't captured on the tape -- in the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn over the page, please, in each document. Or on each version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And, Doctor -- just the first two paragraphs, that will be fine. Doctor, in the first two paragraphs on this page, and take a moment to read them if you need to.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Again, counsel, I'm having difficulty reading them. They are too small for my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: We can fix that, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah, I recall this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In those paragraphs, you set out your interpretation of these events and why they occurred. Please explain that if it requires further explanation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
