utterances.text: Counsel, I don't think these paragraphs require more. They speak for themselves. More so because I was writing it to my boss, and I couldn't leave what I was saying to his guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. In the third paragraph on that page, which is the second paragraph on the top of page 3 of the B/C/S version, Your Honours. You provide some further corroboration for your interpretation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was this the first time you had detected this tension between the military and the political leadership in Belgrade over the peace process?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I can't say it is the first time partly because the nature of the -- of all these issues where civil authorities and military authorities are involved. It is in the nature of these thing that there be tensions. The events usually are troubling. Most of the things are troubling. Honest people can have different points of view. Interests are always varied. Yes, the nature of this is to have tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You spoke earlier of Milosevic being in favour of a settled or a settlement option and other forces or other groups being interested in a war option. Just talking generally now, did that tension always appear to exist as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not chronologically. Events change, players change, interest changed. Except one player from my time there, Milosevic. He was never changed, but I don't think his ideas and positions were static either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can we tender, please, that document as a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Now, before I call up the next document, I'll just check that this time I have it right, Your Honours. 65 ter 03281 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, up until now we were dealing with possible violations that occurred early in February 1995, but you will see here that we have another report related to cross-border flights, this time from, you dated, 1st of March [Realtime transcript read in error, "July"], 1995. You see that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: First of all, in the second paragraph of your report, you link that to emergency medical evacuations from fighting at Mount Vlasic. Can you tell us where Mount Vlasic is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before that, I believe my colleague misspoke himself on line 15, he said the document is dated July 1995. I believe he meant March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I certainly didn't intend July, Your Honours. The 1st of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: But, you see, Doctor, that you refer to fighting at Mount Vlasic near Travnik. Can you tell us where this is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, this way outside my area of operations. The reports coming to me indicated it. I wouldn't be personally as conversant physically in that area as I would where I was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was it -- on whose territory was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This is was in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the context -- if we just turn over to the next page, please, in both versions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: There are three paragraphs I'm interested in. Paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 on both versions. And can you confirm for us that what you've included in those paragraphs is information that were made available to you about the involvement of JA forces?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this paragraph as well as the other one you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. We tender that document as well, Your Honours, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 03282 on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, do you see that again as another -- if we can get it blown up again. Another code cable from you to Mr. Akashi dated 31 March 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You will see from the second paragraph that this deals again with further possible helicopter cross-border violation, this time at the end of March?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And then in the two paragraphs we see the first two paragraphs of the report you link it to activities, military activities, and also refer in paragraph 1 to: "Involvement of the Yugoslav Army on the side of the BSA in the most active and critical battle spots in BiH."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to turn first in the third paragraph, and there you are more specifically referring to the involvement of the 63rd Para-Troop Commando Brigade of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And thereafter in that paragraph, you describe the reason for their involvement, the ABiH. Sorry the army of Herzegovina Bosnia specific targets and so on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, can I tender that document as an Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, to just confirm that these cross border -- possible cross-border flights were investigated to see if they could be substantiated by material taken by the radar tapes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, counsel, the only incident that was subjected to serious investigations rather by those who were reporting it --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: -- was the incident involving the helicopter flights because it became a Security Council issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This was one more of the hundreds of various events that we would report but would not subject to investigation unless there was a reason for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us that in relation to the investigation that was undertaken, those February flights that involve the Security Council, that that investigation was inconclusive?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: To my understanding, it was. But it was done by General Pellnas. The monetary group of the border. The one we discuss earlier. That was the one that was given the mandate for the official investigation. I saw it, I spoke to General Pellnas and it was. I can't prove it, that this happened other than the fact that those who saw the flights vouch that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are the two compatible, those who saw the flights on the one hand and the inconclusive report on the other?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The report said just we saw the flight. If they said they saw them, you don't have other than your eyes physical evidence of what happened. If that physical evidence is missing from the flight observation point of view, and the motivation for doing it is also being disputed, then the only thing you can reach is it's not conclusively determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, did you ever meet General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of General Perisic meeting General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There is an incident that I show in one of my written reports, and it is an incident that occurred as I visited Glina sometime in October, I believe, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause. Where is Glina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Glina is in the former Sector North where I was based, where I had served for longest and the people on the grown I knew them well. As well as the people I used to interact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And October of which year?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I think it's -- unless I check on the report. 1994 or 1995 for me seem to be so blurred, those two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I believe that you are suggesting an answer to the witness. There is no October that's been discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at page 52, line 12. There is the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies. My apologies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you this. Where were you posted at the time that you heard --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I was posted in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: And I was taking a trip back into the sector, I had some business I had to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Now, these authorities, the people I used to meet, knew me well and they knew I was in Belgrade in the capacity I described. So when we met, they took the opportunity to say, Hey, this happened here; and the context was all over the local media, the fallout between the two sides those who were seeking the peace and those who were not seeking the peace was all that they could talk about. It was all about their life, it was whether or not trouble will start back. So they took the opportunity to say even General Perisic was here with Mladic to try to sort out the various oppositions that is were happening including in our part. That was the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Apart from this meeting, are you aware of any other meetings between Mladic and Perisic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are you aware of what sort of relationship existed between Milosevic and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Never met Mladic. But I did meet that many times as my testimony shows with Milosevic. There were issues that involved that would bring him to occasionally say something involving the various parties, and from -- for him, I mean Milosevic to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, if I may just take you a little back. These people who told you that Perisic had come to sort out things with Mladic, did they also tell that you they were present during their meeting, the meeting of the two people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was sure they weren't present, but they said they know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they tell you how they know about the subject of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is because, as I said earlier, this is their life, this is their interest when involved in the peace process. They were involved in negotiating including the contact group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They were, but they don't know what Perisic and Mladic were talking about, do they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They said it was all about this fallout that some of us want to support Milosevic, some of us want not to support it. They are politicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are politicians. What I'm trying to find out from you is whether they had personal knowledge of this or were they just speculating that this is the purpose of the visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't themselves say we were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's clear, there's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they told you the subject of discussion because that subject was general discussion in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was their life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So they were guessing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Guessing about the subject, no. The subject is something that they were involved in. That is, do we support this side or do we support this side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The support Milosevic attempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute. When you say this was something they were involved in, are you talking about Mladic and Perisic or are you talking about the general people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The general people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these people who told you were not party to the meeting between Perisic and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They cannot tell us exactly what they discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, just getting back to Mr. Milosevic and General Mladic, you were talking about your encounters with Mr. Milosevic, and I'm wanting to know from you if from those you are able to tell us what if anything you can of the relationship between Mr. Milosevic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the question is vague as its presently put. What if anything about the relationship, the political relationship, social relationship, psychological relationship. I don't believe the question as put is specifically focused or the witness to be able to really give an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can be more specific, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we deal firstly with the political relationship, are you able to describe that from what you knew from your encounters with Milosevic and others and from your duties?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The most I can say about this, and this is absolutely the most I can say, is that he would comment only when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milosevic. He would make a comment when there is an issue. There's fight, we are trying to stop it, for example. There was a shooting of planes by NATO and the sides that caused it. There are players involved. During those negotiations, he would say what he wanted to say of his view and to let us know his view about these players. One of the reasons we went to see Milosevic plainly speaking was that we believed he had influence with the players associated with any particular event that we are discussing. He would say so and so, this is what I think he is doing, so and so is, I will speak with so and so, and see if we can sort out this issue. Then he will speak either provingly or disapprovingly. I never heard him speak disapprovingly or any -- any way other than differential of Mladic. Very little times it even came out. Very little. So it would be a differential one, if it came at all. But it would be different, for example, in contrast with Karadzic because of his open and public differences or views of the outcome. So that's the most I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that differential note, would it be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It would, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, just before the break you were telling us about what Mr. Milosevic told you about his professional relationship with General Mladic. Did he provide any clues as to his personal relationship with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, at no time would Mr. Milosevic speak personally. He was very, very tuned to the issue of the time, and I wouldn't characterise anything I said about him as any disclosure of anything personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Finally, Doctor, I want to ask you about your time in Belgrade, and specifically your dealings with the FRY political and military leadership there. What I want to ask you is now well informed were they? How informed were they about both political and military events, both in the FRY and outside the FRY?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was my sense of it that they were very informed mostly to the ground about any of the issues and events surrounding whatever it is we came to discuss with them. My sense of it was that they were extremely well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Does that apply to the -- both the political and the military leadership?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever it took or central to the issue. If it was political, that was central to any specific event, they were on top of all details. If there was a military angle to it, they were also very informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Many of the issues that you would have discussed would have been very specific, but necessarily would have needed to have been viewed against a much broader context?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you comment on how well they were informed of the broader issues affecting the whole territory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Let me give you an example. When we were there, my time as representative of the -- special representative of the Secretary-General, I mean delegate of the representative of the Secretary-General, there was a stream of high-level visitors, delegations, both from individual countries, also representing forums, like ICFY. The address was also Mr. Milosevic's office as then-president of Serbia, where that office is located in Belgrade. The issues ranged all the way from broad negotiations of what the outcome would envisage in Bosnia and Herzegovina to the final status and disposition of those areas in Croatia that became known as UNPAs. His reach, his contact was always from the bottom to the top. But the last time, for example, I ended my mandate in there UN staff had been taken hostages in Sarajevo, around Sarajevo. He was involved in the process of getting all these various nationalities released. At the same time, he was negotiating with the American representative, I believe it was Robert Fraser, about the outcome. He was always involved from top to bottom. From the smallest disposition of an issue, to the broader international out come.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you those are all the questions I have for you at this stage. My learned friends for the Defence will have some questions for you, if you kindly answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Thomas. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, if I could have but a moment to set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good. These events --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have a problem, I often drop my voice and the people in the interpretive booth yell at me and rightfully so. I'm wondering can I be heard now just to be sure? If anybody can give me an indication of whether or not my voice is doing all right, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's fine, thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: These events occurred quite a number of years ago, and I'm sure that the situation for you was not only remarkable but also memorable; but as you've said, with regard to some of the details of the matters, that you couldn't remember all of the exact details; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I believe specifically, I was addressing details like sequence of timelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Details like specific dates and specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you gave a statement, I think you probably gave many statements, but you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in September of 1999, about ten years ago, a little give or take a few months?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at that time just would it be fair to say that when you gave that statement, that your memory with regard to the details not only of time, but of certain events was fresher than it is as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You first arrived in the region in April; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before you came to the region, you educated yourself as best you could concerning the situation on the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that particular statement is difficult to place. When you are assigned, Your Honour, a UN mission, you are not supposed to do other than the orientation inside the UN of what the mission is. I had two or three years before been involved in Afghanistan a different situation. It is not a study I'm referred to do nor am I required to know beyond the official terms of reference for the mission. To that extent, I did educate myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say, as you just did, that you are not required to know beyond the official terms of reference for the mission, could you explain to the Chamber what you mean by that specific statement? When you say "official terms of reference"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It's easy to summarise by the enabling resolution putting the mission to action. As it is an international document, it's rather a complete document because the resolution will refer to all the background material that led to the situation, to the reason the Security Council was involved, to the terms of what they want done, and the result they expect. It's rather comprehensive thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your specific research prior or education prior to arriving at Belgrade in April, I take it that you did that? That you educated yourself with regard to reference of the mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, as you've testified here, you understood that there was the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You understood the parameters of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you understood your specific duties and obligations with regard to attempting to effectuate the plan as best you could?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the Vance Plan envisioned both a civil and military component, did it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it had those components.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, part of your duties obviously because I take it you are not a military man, were to liaise with the military component that were involved in the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who found their expression under such organisations as UNPROFOR and the UNMOs; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to the extent that you -- before you arrived once again in Belgrade, to the extent that you knew that you were going to have to liaise with these groups, did you educate yourself with regard to any of the military difficulties that were occurring prior to your arrival? Was that part of your reference?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: If you are talking about educate myself in materials extraneous to what I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. You've told me you didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Upon your arrival to Belgrade, you were immediately seconded to a particular area; correct? Within a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived in that area, did you learn at that point in time upon your arrival as to whether or not your mandate to assist in the effectuation of the Vance Plan was going to be -- I would say hassle-free, but I would say something more subtle than that, which is there were difficulties presented upon your arrival. There were immediate problems in terms of the way that the parties were dealing with the plan as it stood?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That's true. And it was obvious from day one the crossing in the Osijek that we had to do was a battle ground with smouldering tanks with people on both sides; so it wasn't like you had a choice but quickly get an understanding, this is a war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sure that's the case. With regard to the issue of this being a war zone, there was obviously an immediate and direct concern that you had because part of the plan was the notion, and relatively important part of the plan, of demobilising the forces?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The demobilisation of the forces independent of being something that was important on its own, was necessarily connected to the parties' view of what I think you have identified as the opstinas or the municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Partly correct. It was also trying to understand what each of the parties understood we were coming to do. And it was graphically demonstrated to us when we arrived at the confrontation lines in Sector North where one side actually thought we were relief party to take their positions in the foxholes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say one party thought you were to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Relieve them in their positions at the confrontation line in their foxholes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which party was that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the other party, the Croatian side, what was their position with regard to what your mandate -- why you were there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They also figured we are out come there and throw them out of their foxholes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So at the moment that you arrived, there was clearly a severe misunderstanding of what your purpose was that you had to clarify?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which I take it that you did in rapid haste?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We were forced to. One, to say we didn't come to do that, and on the other side, you have to pull back to your positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during those initial days, were there any discussions about precisely which areas, once again I'm talking about the opstinas, were to fall under whose, and I use the word authority in a loose sense for the moment, really what I'm driving at here is if you could explain to the Chamber, the pink zone problem?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I will. And very quickly. Your Honour, this was a culmination of what the learned counsel has been trying to say, that there had to be a clarification of not only our mandate, but also the borders, the jurisdiction borders of that mandate. It was not like most things made by committees, assemblies, watertight. What Vance Plan had said was your mandate will cover these opstinas, and they proceeded to name those opstinas in an annex to his agreement between Belgrade and Zagreb. Those opstinas in the maps that prevailed before the war had boundaries, the civic boundaries of those opstinas. From the Croatian side, they would trace the civic boundaries of those opstinas in their utmost side closest to their side of the war, and trace that as the boundary of where the opstinas would be. That where the UN mandate was to terminate beyond those civic boundary, they didn't expect that we had any mandate regardless of the situation on the ground. From the point of the Serbs, not so. Their interpretation was we have waged this war and we have come to a clear line of confrontation where our forces are deployed. They drew a map tracing that confrontation line and that map often ignored the opstinas boundaries and cut across them. When the two maps are put together, there was an area which became known as pink zones because our military coloured it pink zones because the military mapping itself turned it pink. It became a major issue about those opstinas which were not in the Vance Plan named, and those which the Serbs included because they had waged the war to the border which, if you recall, Your Honour, I said it roughly traces the natural rivers that they wanted to be their natural boundaries. Then because of the dispute about what should be done in those areas where they had a difference of opinion, the matter went all the way to the Security Council and became Resolution 762, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I'd like to read to you from your statement and see whether or not this is a fair, concise summary of that which you just said. And I refer counsel to page 10, which is: "The Vance Plan based the boundaries of the UNPAs," the UNPAs would be the United Nations Protected Areas --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Along the confrontation line as understood by Mr. Cyrus Vance months before the arrival of UNPROFOR In April 1992. The Vance Plan was ambiguous on whether the borders of the UNPAs corresponded to the civic boundaries of the previously demarcated 'opstinas'" -- which is what I think what you were just referring to, "which is apparently what our Croat interlocutors understood, or simply, if the 'borders' of the UNPA reflected the dividing frontline at the time of UNPROFOR's arrival -- which is what the Serb side understood. The areas disputed between the Serb and the Croats eventually became known as the 'pink zones,'" and you've told us why, "the disposition of which became the subject of a specific resolution of the Security Council that essentially amended the original Vance Plan."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm not sure I'm the only one who is hearing noises in their earphones like somebody is rummaging on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I hear noises every once in awhile but I've decided -- I'm glad to know that you hear them too because I thought it was just me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are getting worse and worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see. Let me try something and if this is the noise that you are hearing. Is that the noise you are hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We apologise. I take that upon myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the issue of the pink zones and the amendment to the Vance Plan concerning the pink zones is actually one of the first things that you had to concern yourself with when you arrived in Sector North; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct. Among the many other first things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand there were many first things. When you first got to the area, the political situation was as follows, and I'm talking about in April of 1992: At that point in time FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, had yet to be recognised by anyone, either internally or internationally, as a state; correct.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Croatia, when you arrived, was in the process of recognition, or had they been recognised by then?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They had been recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Bosnia-Herzegovina was up in the air at that time when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There, counsel, I can't be exact. But I do recognise by March of 1992, what was a very peaceful Bosnia had begun to mobilise for war, and the result was their disagreement with the recognition of the declaration of independence of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: So I'm seeking from you the time-line you are thinking about because it was around that time. It too got into this recognition business.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The Republika Srpska was in April had not yet been created?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I hadn't even heard the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the Republika Srpska Krajina once again, was that something that had been created independent of whether or not it had international recognition?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: First time I heard it has to be about May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived, you were -- and by you I mean the UN mission, was relying on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: First few weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would have been consistent, would it not, in your opinion, with the position that had been taken by Milosevic with regard to entering into the Vance Plan, that there was a necessity for the United Nations mission to be there, and they of course were going to need to be supported? Logistically needed support?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The reason was our own failure to get our logistics in order. It was not an expectation that the JNA should provide us with the logistics, but they did. They did it voluntarily and it was appreciated because it would be worse if they fought us, we wouldn't go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, and I think you commented about this in your statement, that it was somewhat ironic that the JNA provided the basics because if they hadn't, the whole mission would have ground to a halt?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It soon became evident, and now I'm moving to the end of April, that the nature of things were going to change dramatically, and by that I mean that among other things, FRY had come into existence, and as a legal matter, I'm not asking you to comment on the legal matter, Doctor; but as a legal matter, you were informed that the authorities in Belgrade understood that by virtue of the fact that now there was a new nation state that had been created, there were certain places that the army, specifically the JNA, could no longer be? And I believe that General Nikovic discussed this with you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that as a matter of fact, was part of the discussion that you had with him when you were working out how the JNA would remove itself from the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, before the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, were there Territorial Defence units in each of the respective republics?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not to my understanding. It was a uniform command called the 10th Corps in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, prior to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, do you know if there was a distinction between the army, the JNA, and groups of individuals who were involved in what we will call Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you were discussing with General Nikovic, and just so we are clear, he was the commander of the JNA and the commander of that entire region; right? When you were discussing the new political reality with General Nikovic - and I'm using some of the language that I found in your statement again because I think it's quite accurate - he indicated that it did not belong in its previous area of responsibility dealing with Croatia as well as with Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were area that they were going to have to leave, and there were a series of practical problems that had to be sorted out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Those are very exact words that he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, did you assist him in your assessment of how to sort out some of these practical problems, or did he come to you with what I'll term as an evacuation plan so that you had an understanding of what the thinking was of the JNA in terms of evacuating the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, we didn't have to entertain that kind of thing. We wanted him to give us a demobilisation as requested by the Security Council, how he is going to do it, and how soon is he going to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at that point in time because there was this issue of those that were born in the area remaining, and those that were not born in the area having to go, the issue of what was going to happen to the assets of the JNA obviously was something of great importance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have discussions with him about what you believed to be in your representative capacity, the most appropriate way of those assets being dealt with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We didn't even to determine that, that was determined for us in the terms of reference for the mission. The terms of reference for the mission required that weapons be demobilised and put into storage in designated areas with one key, symbolic key really, to be held by the mission and the symbolic key to be held by the local authorities. And there, counsel, it is a concession that weapons, some of the weapons it was understood weren't going to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What was clear and what you learned from Lieutenant-General Nikovic was it was the intention of the JNA to leave behind and I'm quoting from your statement again and see whether or not this is an accurate quote, "A clear and clean situation militarily and administratively."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he gave you a full account of how the JNA and TDF units were previously deployed into different groups; he focused on the withdraw of the JNA in handing over military control to UNPROFOR. And your estimation at that time, it would be fair to say, would it not, that he, the general of the JNA appeared surprisingly forthcoming both in substance and in attitude?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was cooperative?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he was as a representative of the JNA well disposed to seeing that the United Nations mandate was implemented fairly and in full?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did he say something to the effect of, and I quote, Therefore what UNPROFOR agrees with Belgrade will apply to Serbia Krajina.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I took that to mean he is going to make a proposal of how to leave what you just referred to as a clear and clean situation because he was requested by us, but his channels were different than ours. Our channels go through the force commander of the UN. His went to Belgrade. When that proposal that is developed from the ground is accepted, what disagreed would then apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as you said some ten years ago, one of the other parties to this, however, had a slightly different view. And you said as it turned out, however, the local Serbs had a different agenda?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to talk for a minute about that different agenda, if I could. You learned that they intended to consolidate their own whole on the contested territory in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you learned that, is that a reference to the UNPAs, or is that a bit more far reaching than the UNPAs or the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I meant what they themselves considered the extent of something they called Republika Srpska Krajina, and that extended in all of the sectors: north, south, Slavonia, west Slavonia, inclusive of the pink zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I may have got the wrong impression from your testimony earlier today, and if I did, please correct me; and if I didn't then you can help here, which is, I was led to believe that it was your view that what happened was that the Territorial Defence forces just were set up by the JNA, and when the JNA left it was your position that the Territorial Defence forces was what the JNA left in situ as it were? Is that what you said? Is that a fair rendition of what you said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you if this is a fair rendition then of what actually occurred in your estimation, which is that the local Serbs found a loop-hole in the Vance Plan. And the loop-hole in the Vance Plan was one that excluded police units from the armed group that were to be demobilised?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So what happened then is that the local Serbs, the local Serbs proceeded to set up their "Territorial Defence forces (TDF)," right at the heels of the JNA withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. It's not the JNA that set them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was the local Serbs that set this up. So the Vance Plan as constituted unfortunately had not one ambiguity which was the one we spoke to with regard to the pink zone, but there was another ambiguity here which is how does one define a police force?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I'm not sure, counsel, I ambiguity and loop-hole are synonymous. Because that's where you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The loop-hole they found is not an ambiguity, it's a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So it's worse?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'll put it to you in another term, then. There were, at least up until this point, in the discussion of the Vance Plan, there were two structural difficulties that allowed for interpretation and/or misinterpretation with regard to how to achieve its purpose?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, even with the problems that were created in terms of the structural difficulties that existed, in your capacity, you never received any resistance from Belgrade with regard to trying to continue to implement the Vance Plan, did you? I mean, you never were in a situation where you received information, for example, from Milosevic where he throws up his hands and says, Listen, this plan is full of holes, we can't make this work, let's go back to the drawing table?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, not in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you first got there, once again I'm now referring to Sector North, you had occasion to deal with a gentleman by the name of Lazarevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I notice the smile on your face, and I take it that the dealings with this particular individual were less than satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In all respects. He was -- would it be fair to say he was a scoundrel at best?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He was a thorn in our flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not someone you can rely on too terribly much?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It took us awhile to figure that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you as you sit here today recall when the JNA finally withdrew from the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Let me say this: We went with the difficulties up to a point where we were happy we had reached a demobilisation. The weapons were handed over. We had designated storage points. The remnants of JNA who were born there were in civilian uniform, and the militia which is a local term for the police were in the blue uniform, and for awhile there was an air that we are getting somewhere with this Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is a civilian uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blue, blue uniforms as opposed to the military fatigue. Fatigues that military, you know, all the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you said: "We had designated storage points, the remnants of the JNA who were born there were in civilian uniform, and the militia which is a local form for the police were in the blue uniform."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm quoting what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, what is civilian uniform as distinct from the blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant civilian clothes like you and me, not even a uniform at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were in their suits and they were in their casuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They were in mufti, in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to get some clarity on another brief issue, which is that when you were speaking with General Nikovic concerning the new political reality, he told you that there would be six countries created from the former Yugoslavia, and he proceeded to name them specifically as follows: Slovenia, Croatia, the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia, and Montenegro being included in that - for that I was doing the parenthetical remark - the Serbian Krajina, Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I want to move forward now, if I could, to this whole issue concerning what I'm going to call generally speaking the helicopters and the tapes, which have a series of component parts obviously, and we'll talk about the various component parts. But as an initial matter - so that we are all very clear - the idea was that at the Surcin airport, there would be observers from United Nations military observers present in the room to make a determination as to whether or not everything was okay or whether or not there were, in fact, violations. And if there were violations, the importance of that was twofold or maybe even more than that, but certainly the importance of violations were something that needed to be immediately reported because of the concern that had been expressed in the resolution about no-fly zones. And second of all, there was also at that time another issue which is whether or not sanctions which had been previously imposed would remain, would increase, or would lessen, because sanctions, as a matter of fact, were one of the true bargaining chips that you had, and when I say you, I mean United Nations had at its disposal in terms of trying to regulate, and I use the word advisedly, but I think it's a fair word, to regulate the madness at the time.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt. Apart from the stenographer is there anybody else who is typing or moving around with a mouse?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am. I was making a joke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know whether I'm the only one but there is just this noise in the earphones that --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I must confess that I was, but it shouldn't be picked up. The microphones are off here, but if it's being picked up, then we'll stay away from keyboards and mousses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would appreciate if that could happen because it looks like my microphone is extra sharp today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm with you. I'm having the same issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, one of the natural consequences of the sanctions that were imposed were that certain items that were necessary to make the radar function were not available in the radar room?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A claim was made to that effect, and I underscore the word, a claim was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the claim that was made to that effect, was a claim made to the effect that certain of the machines in the room had to be cannibalised in order to make other machines work? And by cannibalised, I mean they were taken apart so that you could have a couple of operative machines?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I think I heard something to that effect, but it came in a context that made me -- made it hard for me because for that you don't have to make sure that are UNMOs are not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, initially isn't what occurred that -- and I'm trying to see whether or not because I think you reflect this in one of your reports, but an animosity kind of built up; there was tension.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There was a tension in the workplace, too many people in a small room, and there were a lot of extraneous issues and somebody got mad and acted badly. It had great international effect, but I'm trying to stay in the room for the moment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because initially what happened was that the UNMO observing station was taken over by one else, and the observer was no longer at a station in particular but was able to peer over someone's shoulder; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, those two details for me since I wasn't presently there to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to go back then to -- just for a moment to see if we can clarify this, and it's the -- it's P472.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have P472 up on the screen, please, and I'm referring to page, I believe it's 8 of 10. And I'd like to go to the very first line entry which is 1 February 1995. And the very first entry. If you could make that larger for Dr. Kirudja, please, so he doesn't have to squint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It says: "The supervisor switched off the screen used by the UNMO from this moment only 'over-shouldering, over-shoulder monitoring' was permitted."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that means what I'm talking about is a practical effect apart from the inter-radar room politics that were going on, from a practical effect, the UNMO had the ability to monitor although not in the fashion that had been envisioned?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Can you, counsel, be sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm saying just by basis of the sitrep that we received that he had over-shoulder monitoring?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking. If I'm required to be in front of it for monitoring, I'm no longer in front of it. Maybe I can cast a glance. Can you conclude I'm monitoring?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair comment. Fair comment. Looking later, going back to the page again looking further down, if we could, 7 until 10 it says: "UNMO have no access to any screen and is restricted to sit at the writing desk next to the supervisor." Could you help us there? Is the supervisor the UNMO is sitting next to an UNMO supervisor or is it a radar -- someone in the radar?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, I went out read easily there is a supervisor of this facility. It's a government facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So while he is while the UNMO is at the writing desk for that period of time, it would seem that there may not be any over-the-shoulder monitoring ability?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's obviously a distinction between at least in the author's mind who put the sitrep together for your information to forward on, that a there is a distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank goodness ultimately the whole issue is resolved.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the way that it's resolved is that there is an analysis of the tapes. Do you know if they ever got the spare parts?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: As I said to you earlier, after the whole thing was sorted out, there was no talk of spare parts. The machines were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So this could all be attributed to bad mood in the work environment which obtained international dimension, unfortunately?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, counsel. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the tape analysis that occurred, the tape analysis ultimately revealed, if you recall, and if not there's some documents we can pull up, but ultimately revealed a couple of thing that is had been maintained by the authorities at FRY for sometime, that in fact there were some flights. And those flights were, in fact, countenanced flights, I believe there were four medical flights, four humanitarian flights, and two evacuation flights.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Certainly, counsel, it's better to check the document more accurately. My memory of it was that there were something they called traces seen on the tapes. There was a reference to some traces that they couldn't discern or what they were. But it is also a record that -- an evaluation says there was some flights. If this was the flight seen by the Dutch soldiers or some of the things that you have referred to early on, it is not certain. That's my recollection but it's certainly a good thing to be clear about what the report says, and I know you have it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We will get to that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have, I believe, it's page 6 of that -- page 6 of the report for a quick second. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to the observations that you made on the 13th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have paragraph 13 made a little bit bigger so those of us who are older can see better. I fortunately have my glasses on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "It is evident from the above that the FRY authority have provided not new information, but new arguments in support of those inclined to back their position at the SC." Could you tell us what SC means?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. "From their viewpoint, they're innocent until proven to the contrary. Further they are clearly putting out the signal that they too have not lost the right not to be compelled to be witness against themselves. They have left, however, the door open to patching up the quarrel started by the hitherto unidentified supervisors ordering the UNMOs away from the radar screens. This situation will probably be fixed in a couple of days." Those were your observations at the time. And with regard to in support of those inclined to back their position to Security Council, I take it what you are referring to is that there were certain members of the Security Council at the time who were of the position, specifically the Russian Federation that you mention on page 3 of this report, who were in a line with and supported the position, the general position taken here of not being compelled to be witness against themselves?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, you are right generally in your surmise, but I want this paragraph to be understood it's not really conjecture, and me musing about what happened. I did actually have a discussion of those views expressed on paragraph 13 with Mr. Cicanovic, who was the head of the foreign minister dealing with this matter in the Security Council. And he put it very clearly that we take the position there were no flights. And if anyone else has proof we had is up to someone else to provide us with the information or with the evidence. So it's not as speculative as it might seem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You just used the term -- I'm done with that particular exhibit thank you so much. You just used the term "surmise," and I appreciate that you did because if I understand the sequence of events with the recognition that the document that we just dealt with was issued by you on the 13th of February. On the 16th of February, which is document you authored, we've discussed briefly before, that's P473, which we'll get to, the subject is, "The helicopter flights, a maybe epilogue."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you use as a basis for some of your musings, and I'm not using the term in an insulting fashion, but I think rather one in which you went through a deductive process based upon the information that you had, that the helicopter flights, in fact, were an indication of a crack, if I might, in the political stability of Milosevic's position?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Strategy, not position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And that you believe, and if we could have the document up, that would be nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page 2. First paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You state that: "Surprisingly all pieces of this story, rather incredulously, I might admit, to the episode as being an internal affair by the JA calculated to send a daring message to Milosevic. That message has to do with the efforts of the international mediators trying to get Milosevic to agree to a package involving the recognition of Croatia/Bosnia-Herzegovina and the lifting of sanctions." Now, I want to pause here for a moment, and at this time have some of the following discussion with you, which is: Did you have confidential source information that you were relying upon to -- independent of what we see here that is of assistance to you in this deductive process that you are going through?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I had a variety of sources, Your Honour, in writing this report. When I look at them, I have to remind myself especially the document itself, the one you are referring to, as contrasted with the document you referred earlier in your comment prepared in New York in the whole testimony. That was prepared for testimony to this court. This document was not prepared for testimony in a court. It was not a document that intended to be reviewed other than by it's recipient in a confidential manner. We had, therefore, many sources, and the intention of even what is there, the content, is to improve our discussions and negotiations with FRY authorities so that we -- if we knew or thought we knew what the reasons behind things were, so much for our negotiations. Therefore, the sources which I discussed and used included the totality of what was available to us, first in our normal flow, military, civil, as well as civilian sources. And some of them were private in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this specific matter, you say here, it's -- if you go down to the bottom of this particular page, please: "Three days ago my sources further inform me ..." Could you tell us which sources those were.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say no, not now, I mean --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: What date is this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document is the 16th of February, 1995, so a long time ago. I understand.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So as you sit here today, you don't recall who those sources were.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, and since I didn't want to identify them, it remains vague and I wouldn't want to speculate now because I would have then to tell you which part of this report came from who, and I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's like a double-key system?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yeah, almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Three days ago my sources further informed me, a letter signed by some 80 JA generals and colonels began to circulate." Did you ever see such a letter?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I remember this would appear in the local language and usually for all my sources, I reply on interpretation and translation. So originals of this kind of thing are not something that I would know about. So if somebody transcribed it and brought it to us, then that is all we needed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So then as you sit here today, you don't recall ever seeing such a letter?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the letter you further go on to say: "It reportedly warns Milosevic that if he recognises Croatia and BiH and therefore, disowns the RSK and the RS, they will disobey the supreme council and commander and join the fighting forces of these two Serb states." Now, before we go any further, in 1995, do you know who was the Chief of Staff and head commander of the Yugoslav Army? I may be able to help you out, that was this gentleman here, Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I was going to tell you because I was dealing with this liaison, a Colonel Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Vuksic, yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what you are referring to there when you refer to the commander, that is the commander that you are referring to, isn't it? And the reason I'm asking you that question is because in the statement that you prepared some ten years ago concerning this matter, for purposes of testifying, as you've told us, the language that you used is as follows: "... they would disobey the Supreme Defence Council and the JA commander." So you've defined it, and "... joined the military forces of the RSK and RS." That's on page 59 of your statement for purposes of counsel.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, that piece of information there is a piece of information, as I understand it, that was based upon somebody else's giving you an idea of what was going on? You never saw a document that established that there were 80 generals who said this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, part of the importance of your surmise on this issue of what I'm discussing is the Milosevic -- I am going to call it the Milosevic dilemma, if I might, at the time was based directly upon the issue of the helicopters. They were tied into each other as you thought of at the time; correct? That's what it seemed to be at the time for you. You had the suspicious helicopter incidents, you reported about it on the 13th of February, and on the 16th of February, you are dealing with a helicopter incidents as well as this other piece of information that you believe exists with regard to the general's letter, so you are seeing at that point in time in your mind some schism that's occurring that is of importance for purposes of internal understanding for further negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct. But I would like to rephrase that, it is more or less the last piece of a puzzle originating for a longer period, and there were other pieces of that puzzle --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: -- that are not mentioned or summarised, but those you have summarised are part and parcel of the collage of these pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in your mind, in your mind, what was the -- the importance of this particular information from the standpoint of the sensitivity of the international negotiations that are going on at the time? Because, as I read it, it seems as if we are at a very delicate, in your estimation, we are at a very delicate point in terms of how to proceed forward.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And was part of the concern then a concern about how best to assist Milosevic and obviously Perisic because you include him in achieving the peace based upon the information you believe to be true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Actually, nowhere in my testimony would indicate, since I don't believe I had reached any conclusion, which side of this divide that you are describing he fell, your client fell, into. There's nothing in that testimony that would allude to that, nor do I think I ever, to this day, made up an understanding of which side of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me go back then to the other issue that I was -- raised with you before, because perhaps we need some clarification. Which is on page 59 of your statement, you say, the one that you prepared for testimony, you say: "Indeed, three days prior to the aforementioned flights into Srebrenica, 80 JA generals and colonels publicly warned Milosevic that if he recognised Croatia in BiH - thereby disowning the RSK and RS - they would disobey the Supreme Defence Council and the," and I place the emphasis here, "JA commander."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would have been General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. That's assuming that it's true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that your information is accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm a minute before what I believe would be an appropriate time. Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you still have some more questions to ask. Are you moving on to a new topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would be moving on to a new topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break and adjourn for the day tomorrow morning at 9.00 in courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th of January 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.
